data.title: Numbers Show More Biotech Sponsors Turn to Kivo to Keep TMFs and Assets Diligence-Ready
data.description:
PORTLAND, Ore. —

Kivo, the GxP-compliant document and process management platform for life sciences teams, today announced over 200 percent growth in biotech sponsors keeping their trial master files (TMFs) and regulatory assets on its platform, as more clinical-stage companies adopt its GxP-compliant solution to increase attractiveness to investors and acquirers. Sponsors now manage more than 3,000 drug programs in Kivo.

Kivo supports drug programs throughout their journey, from preclinical development through Phase 1, Phase 2, and Phase 3 clinical trials and ultimately toward regulatory approval, partnership, or acquisition. By bringing Regulatory, Clinical, and Quality operations together, Kivo helps ensure that the data and documents surrounding an asset are always ready for audits, inspections, and due diligence.

“Having more than 3,000 drug programs managed in Kivo represents a real shift in the industry,” said Toban Zolman, CEO of Kivo. “Guiding drugs through testing and approval is hard enough. The systems behind it shouldn’t make it harder. Our job is to remove the friction from GxP compliance so teams can focus on advancing great science and getting it closer to patients.”

Kivo Customers Landed $3 Billion in Investment in the Last Year 

In today's investment climate, maintaining diligence-ready documents creates a distinct advantage. Early-stage biotechs are increasingly choosing to manage their assets in a validated, GxP-compliant system from the start, rather than trying to store and share their pre-clinical documents and data rooms from a file-sharing system.

In the last year alone, customers of Kivo attracted more than $3 billion in investment capital, citing this as one of their reasons for growth. 

This reinforces the importance of keeping a drug program ready throughout its lifecycle, as investment rounds, partnership discussions, due diligence, and acquisition opportunities arise. Having the underlying documents, data, and regulated processes organized and ready helps teams move more quickly in these circumstances.

More Sponsors are Using Kivo to Take Ownership of the TMF

More sponsors are also bringing their TMFs into Kivo, either to manage active trials directly or to take custody of the TMF from their CRO at study close. In addition to the need for inspection readiness, the shift also reflects the impact of the ICH E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice guideline, adopted by the FDA last year, which reinforces that sponsors remain responsible for, and should maintain control of, their essential trial records and data. 

As a member of the CDISC Vendor Committee, Kivo has also participated in the development of the new TMF Reference Model standard. Kivo will host a webinar on the TMF Reference Model on Thursday, November 12. Register here to attend: Unpacking TMF Standard Model V1.

See what's behind the momentum with a self-guided tour of the Kivo platform.

data.title: Biopharma likely to climb higher after ‘blue wave,’ analysts say
data.description:
The midterm elections have swung control of U.S. Congress from one side of the aisle to another, as Democrats on Tuesday regained majorities in the House and Senate. And that shift is likely to escalate, rather than hinder, the biopharmaceutical sector’s broader recovery, according to Wall Street analysts.

Drug pricing may not be the hot-button issue it has been after past elections, given that former president Joe Biden and President Donald Trump have both implemented programs and deals to control their growth.

In particular, the number of drugs subject to Medicare price negotiation under the Biden-era “Inflation Reduction Act” is set to automatically expand each year, meaning lawmakers don’t need to intervene to ensure its effects. The IRA is also seen by Democrats as their “big victory on drug pricing” and “too complicated to materially change,” said RBC Capital Markets analyst Brian Abrahams, at a recent media briefing.

Nor is it expected that Democrats will meaningfully tinker with Trump’s “most-favored nation” drug pricing deals, which offered tariff relief in return for lowering U.S. pharmaceutical costs. Those pacts haven’t meaningfully affected drugmaker bottom lines, but they’ve helped boost access to certain medicines — like obesity drugs for Medicare recipients.

“I think the agreements are signed and are going until the end of the term of this government,” Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla said during an earnings call on Tuesday.

Democrats could probe these “tariff-avoidance” deals next year, but likely have “bigger fish to fry” than drug pricing, wrote Leerink Partners analyst David Risinger. A better bet is the issue returning in full force ahead of the next presidential election, he added.

Analysts also expect greater scrutiny of leadership at the Food and Drug Administration as well as the Department of Health and Human Services, both of which have had a tumultuous start in Trump’s second term.

The Senate, for instance, still has to deal with the pending confirmation of Heidi Overton, Trump’s nominee for FDA commissioner. That vote would need to occur in a lame duck session, or Overton’s nomination might expire once Congress adjourns for the year — giving newly sworn-in Democrats a greater chance to impact her appointment.

Biotech investors and analysts view Overton’s nomination as further entrenching the kind of steadiness that’s taken hold at the FDA after the turbulent tenure of Marty Makary, who was castigated for erratic agency decision-making that frustrated the industry. The FDA has since reversed many of its controversial Makary-era rulings, and its two main drug review offices are now headed by permanent replacements. Overton’s confirmation would complete the staffing cycle.

“The new leadership regime at the FDA looks like it is tracking towards more stability and I would say reasonable flexibility,” said RBC’s Abrahams.

Vaccine policy could become a target, too, following a series of moves by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that weakened recommendations for immunizations and have been sharply criticized by the medical establishment.

Many elected Democrats “voiced their support for proven medical science,” Risinger wrote. That suggests Kennedy could be under greater pressure and certain aspects of the “MAHA” movement, such as attacks on vaccines, “could face scrutiny.”

The next Congress may take a closer look at a recent and notable shift in the global pharmaceutical pipeline, zeroing in on a surge in collaborations involving drugs originating from China. The Treasury Department recently proposed adding biotech to the “COINS” Act, which could curtail certain U.S. investments in China.

The RBC team argued that, while there’s bipartisan agreement China poses a threat to the U.S. pharmaceutical sector, the concerns are “overstated.” Any future action is likely to be focused on protecting U.S. patient data and safety, and shielding intellectual property from the Chinese military, said analyst Leonid Timashev.

“What we're not expecting is a blanket ban on data from China. We’re expecting a ban on manufacturing. We're not expecting a ban on M&A or things like that,” he said.

The sector’s early stock performance on Wednesday suggests investors are optimistic. The XBI, a stock fund correlated with the industry’s health, ticked up by a percentage point before trading essentially flat Wednesday morning. That aligns with historical data, according to Jefferies analyst Faisal Khurshid. The XBI has generated positive returns in the six months following each of the last four midterm elections, he wrote in a Tuesday client note.

Khurshid’s team doesn’t see the midterms being as “impactful” to biotech as presidential elections. Sentiment will be much more dependent on dealmaking and the state of FDA leadership, which now seems “industry-supportive,” he wrote.

data.title: START Expands its Global Early Phase Cancer Site Network into Italy Through Strategic Partnership with Istituti Fisioterapici Ospitalieri
data.description:
SAN ANTONIO —

The START Center for Cancer Research (“START”), the largest global network of fully dedicated early-phase oncology clinical trial sites, and Istituti Fisioterapici Ospitalieri (“IFO”), the public research hospital organization in Rome that includes IRCCS Istituto Nazionale Tumori Regina Elena, today announced a strategic partnership to establish a new START early-phase clinical trial site within the Regina Elena National Cancer Institute. The collaboration is intended to expand opportunities for eligible patients in Rome, the Lazio region and across Italy to gain access to novel investigational cancer therapies through clinical trials.

 

Recognized by the Italian Ministry of Health as an Istituto di Ricovero e Cura a Carattere Scientifico (IRCCS), Regina Elena serves patients from Rome and the Lazio region, as well as patients referred from other regions of Italy and abroad. The institute combines cancer diagnosis, treatment and research, with expertise spanning major adult solid tumors, hematological malignancies and rare cancers. IFO also includes the San Gallicano Dermatological Institute, which specializes in dermatological diseases. 

 

Italy records approximately 390,000 new cancer diagnoses a year, according to the 2025 edition of the national report “I numeri del cancro in Italia,” produced by AIOM and partner organizations. By bringing early-phase research into an established cancer institute, the partnership aims to make trial evaluation more closely connected with patients’ existing oncology care.

 

Despite this significant cancer burden, Italy has a lower number of clinical trials relative to its population than several major Western European markets, highlighting an opportunity to expand clinical research activity and offer sponsors greater access to patients through established research institutions.

 

The partnership pairs START’s experience running early-phase oncology trials with IFO’s clinical and translational research capabilities. The Rome site will be START’s first in Italy, extending its global community-based site network into an important oncology market. It will give patients, their families, and their physicians more clinical trial options as part of the continuum of care and give sponsors a new country through which to benefit from START’s global network.

 

“Italy has a substantial cancer burden and world-class institutions, yet clinical trial activity relative to population remains lower than in several other major European markets,” said Nick Slack, MBE, Chairman and CEO of START. “By partnering with IFO and the Regina Elena National Cancer Institute, an established leader in Italian cancer care and research, we can bring early-phase oncology research closer to patients across Italy and advance our mission of providing Hope Through Access.”

 

“As a national cancer institute serving patients in Rome, Lazio, across Italy and internationally, we see this partnership as an opportunity to connect more patients with early-phase clinical research while strengthening the integration of care and innovation,” said Livio De Angelis, Director General of IFO. 

 

“Combining Regina Elena’s multidisciplinary clinical and scientific expertise with START’s early-phase trial network can create new opportunities for collaboration and clinical research across a broad range of cancers,” said Giovanni Blandino, Scientific Director, IRCCS Istituto Nazionale Tumori Regina Elena.

 

Across its two institutes, IFO records on average about 10,000 inpatient and day-hospital admissions and more than 1.275 million outpatient services a year. Regina Elena belongs to the European Reference Network for adult solid cancers and is a member of Alleanza Contro il Cancro, the alliance of Italian IRCCS cancer centers. 

 

START currently operates the largest global network of early-phase clinical trial sites, with more than 45 Principal Investigators across 17 locations in the United States and Europe. With nearly 1,000 active studies, START provides access to one of the most extensive portfolios of industry-sponsored early-phase cancer trials worldwide. The new IFO site will be fully integrated into the START network, with access to its global trial portfolio from day one.

data.title: Earnings roundup: AstraZeneca’s cost cuts, Alnylam’s slump and Regeneron’s resilience
data.description:
With quarterly earnings underway, BioPharma Dive is providing a snapshot of some companies’ results and how they’re being received by investors. Today, we’re offering insight into the latest numbers from AstraZeneca, Alnylam Pharmaceuticals and Regeneron Pharmaceuticals.

AstraZeneca’s cost cuts

Since 2024, AstraZeneca has zeroed in on a key number: $80 billion. Executives have been adamant full-year revenue will hit that target by 2030, even in the face of multiple clinical setbacks that have slowed the company’s momentum.

AstraZeneca reiterated in its latest earnings report it is “on track” to meet that goal. Since February, the company has reported positive results from 12 late-stage programs and brought four new drugs to market, CEO Pascal Soriot told analysts. Over the next year, 20 “high-value trial readouts” could, if positive, yield peak annual revenue opportunities surpassing $20 billion.

“A significant part” of that total should “become reality over the next few years,” Soriot proclaimed.

Yet a different number — $1.5 billion — caught Wall Street’s attention on Friday. That’s a figure associated with a new cost-savings program, “Reshaping for Sustainable Growth,” that AstraZeneca revealed alongside its June-to-September results. Through it, the company will save $1.5 billion annually and “reinvest” that money largely back into drug research, according to a presentation.

When speaking with analysts, CEO Soriot claimed AstraZeneca has been working on this plan since the beginning of the year. The company believes it has to “redeploy resources” to support its pipeline, in part by embedding artificial intelligence more deeply into its operations, he said.

AI is helping “make us faster, smarter,” Soriot said. AstraZeneca can “grow without growing,” meaning it can “grow without adding as many people as you would have if you didn't have the use of AI.”

Finance chief Aradhana Sarin reportedly said on a separate media call that she doesn’t expect the initiative to lead to a net reduction in the size of AstraZeneca’s workforce. The company projects a one-time $2 billion restructuring charge in connection with the program.

AstraZeneca shares climbed 7% on Friday.

Alnylam’s slump

Two years ago, Alnylam Pharmaceuticals triumphantly declared that Amvuttra, a drug critical to its future, succeeded in an important trial in a deadly heart disease. To Wall Street, the result made Amvuttra a surefire blockbuster and positioned Alnylam for profitability. Company shares rocketed from around $160 in June 2024 to record highs of more than $480 as Amvuttra’s launch in that disease, transthyretin amyloidosis cardiomyopathy, got off to a very fast start.

With the release of its latest earnings report on Thursday, though, Alnylam has now given all of that value back. Earlier this year, the company cut guidance after conceding that Amvuttra’s early launch spike benefited from pent-up demand that’s since normalized. And though Alnylam on Thursday reported $1.13 billion in third-quarter Amvuttra revenue — in line with Wall Street expectations — investors came away even more skeptical of its sales trajectory.

Analysts believe one reason for the cynicism is a proposed rule change that, if finalized, would substantially cut Medicare reimbursement for medicines acquired through the 340B drug discount program. Another is that UnitedHealth, one of the nation’s largest insurers, adopted a more “restrictive” policy for first-line Amvuttra use in certain patients. These disclosures reflected a “weaker-than-anticipated outlook” for Amvuttra and heightened the chances that the drug’s 2026 revenue ends up on the lower end of Alnylam’s financial forecasts, wrote William Blair analyst Myles Minter.

“The back-to-back quarters of headwinds undoubtedly call into question the growth outlook for the franchise and make it difficult to assess near-term 2027 revenue estimates as well as the longer-term trajectory,” Minter added.

Alnylam shares tumbled more than 20% as investors digested the news and its implications for Amvuttra. The near-term numbers for the drug “are likely to come down — probably significantly,” wrote Stifel analyst Paul Matteis. “[I]t’s hard to see a path for the stock with it not being a beat-and-raise story.”

Regeneron’s resilience

Regeneron Pharmaceuticals’ outlook appeared shaky only months ago. A procession of newly launched biosimilar medicines posed a budding threat to its Eylea eye drug business. A high-dose form of Eylea wasn’t selling as well as investors had hoped. And a top oncology prospect fell short in an anticipated study in melanoma, wiping out a revenue opportunity the company had been counting on. In early June, shares traded around $612 apiece, their lowest levels since late last year. Some analysts called on management to make a deal to change the narrative.

Yet Regeneron’s market value has steadily crept back up since then. And on Friday, shares shot up by another 13% on an earnings report lauded by Wall Street analysts. Between June and September, global net sales of top moneymaker Dupixent spiked 35% to $6.5 billion — and Regeneron is now seeing more of that cash after wrapping up research payments it had owed to partner Sanofi. High-dose Eylea generated $700 million, topping Wall Street estimates. The cancer immunotherapy Libtayo followed with $550 million, also beating expectations.

All three numbers represented record totals, which “underscores the health of Regeneron’s core businesses” and reflects the company’s “successful defense” against biosimilar competition, wrote RBC Capital Markets analyst Brian Abrahams in a Friday note. Investors are “undoubtedly rewarding this performance.”

“Biosimilar and branded competition to Eylea is still worth watching for '27,” Abrahams wrote. But “for now we expect the headline beat to dominate optics.”

TD Cowen analyst Tyler Van Buren added that Regeneron’s drug pipeline, which includes an autoimmune therapy in late-stage testing, a blood thinner in Phase 3 trials and a longer-acting form of Dupixent “continues to see very little value” from investors.

One prospect he and others are watching is an RNA-based medicine Regeneron licensed from Alnylam. Regeneron is developing the drug, “ALN-CIDEB,” for the liver disease “MASH.” On a Friday conference call, executives described the drug’s effects on liver-fat levels in an early-stage trial as “game-changing,” though Regeneron hasn’t yet proved that the treatment can affect the inflammation and scarring that characterizes the disease.

The drug appears “differentiated,” but “we think it is premature to call CIDEB’s efficacy best-in-class,” wrote Leerink Partners analyst David Risinger.

Early data will be presented at a medical meeting this month. Phase 3 testing should start by the end of the year.

data.title: Keytruda biosimilars are coming — but they face an uphill battle
data.description:
The Keytruda biosimilars are coming.

In October, the FDA accepted the first publicly announced application for a Keytruda copycat dubbed FYB206, which it could approve as early as the third quarter of 2027. About a dozen other candidates are also in the works, as Keytruda approaches a patent cliff and key expirations begin in 2028.

An FDA nod for FYB206 will open the door to competition for the world’s bestselling cancer drug, which brought in $31.7 billion for Merck & Co. in 2025.

Even so, the path to growth for these biosimilars may be uphill.

Branded manufacturers often make strategic deals with PBMs and other stakeholders along the pharmaceutical supply chain, which can create financial incentives that favor the established products, Michael Abrams, managing partner at Numerof & Associates, pointed out.

“What we have at a macro level is the sum total of a lot of deals, many of which I think are probably anti-competitive,” he said. “Most of which are so well hidden that nobody is in a position to evaluate them. And so we have a system that works in favor of the established status quo.”

Without unwinding this tangle of deals between drug companies, PBMs, insurance companies, pharmacies and hospitals, there’s little chance of a market in which competition reliably translates into lower consumer costs, Abrams said. And this complex web that favors branded drugs could prevent Keytruda biosimilars from taking off.
 

Regulatory support collides with market hurdles

An estimated 118 biologic medicines, representing about $232 billion in potential sales, currently stand to lose patent protection by 2034. That doesn’t mean their biosimilars will take over the market. And the challenges their biosimilars will face in the marketplace come despite federal efforts to smooth the path to market for these drugs, Abrams said.

For example, the FDA’s Biosimilars Action Plan, first released in 2018, outlined strategies to support biosimilar development and market adoption.

FYB206’s developer Formycon and partner Zydus Lifesciences Limited, which was tapped to commercialize the product in the U.S. and Canada, said the FDA agreed with the company on a development pathway that didn’t require a comparative phase 3 efficacy trial.

“This enabled us to accelerate the program and substantially reduce development investment while maintaining the rigorous scientific standards required for biosimilar approval,” Dr. Stefan Glombitza, CEO of Formycon, stated in a press release.

Abrams said this could set a precedent for other products, provided the approval goes smoothly.

“The FDA and the sponsor had to agree on tests and measures that would be reported to FDA to assess whether this biosimilar is as safe and as effective as the reference product,” he said. “And if it goes as they anticipated, this will get approved and the precedent will stand, and then other biosimilars can follow that same path.”

But there are still questions hanging over which indications FYB206 could be approved for. Keytruda has notched FDA nods in over 30 indications to date.

“If FYB206 is approved as a biosimilar to Keytruda (pembrolizumab), theoretically it could receive approval for virtually all of Keytruda's indications without conducting separate clinical trials in each cancer type,” Abrams said. “However, some indications could still be excluded if Keytruda’s indication has unexpired orphan-drug exclusivity or other protections that prevent FDA approval of a biosimilar for those uses.”

Formycon and Zydus might opt to omit certain indications to avoid infringement disputes, or the FDA might require additional evidence for some uses, he added.

While the companies may be able to get the drug approved faster thanks to regulatory tailwinds, that might not be the biggest hurdle for any incoming biosimilar — a situation that could dissuade more biosimilar development down the road.

“If nobody wants to buy [FYB206] because the system is rigged against it, [companies] aren’t going to line up to develop biosimilars even if [development] is a little cheaper and faster,” Abrams said.

Consumers often pay high prices for brand-name biologics, which make up an estimated 5% of prescriptions, but 51% of drug spending, according to the FDA.

To help offset these costs, the FDA has approved more than 85 biosimilars to date. Biosimilars Forum, a nonprofit industry advocacy group, credits these drugs with saving the U.S. healthcare system some $56 billion, and says they have the potential to save as much as $181 billion more in the next five years because the drugs, on average, cost half the price of brand-name options.

But the market share for biosimilars remains below 20%, even though they’re evaluated for safety and efficacy, according to the FDA.

“These savings are being completely left on the table because PBMs have prioritized in their formularies high-cost, high-rebate drugs over lower-cost biosimilars,” Biosimilars Forum states on its website.

The organization is advocating for measures such as PBM reform and other policies that remove competitive barriers to increase access to these drugs.

Changing those market factors will be a big challenge for legislators, largely because of the system’s complexity, Abrams said.

“We don’t have anybody who is expert enough who follows this on a regular basis or can speak with credibility about what’s really going on,” Abrams said.

Legislation aimed at leveling the playing field has really just nibbled around the edges of the issue so far, he said.

For now, companies will likely be watching this potential first Keytruda biosimilar test case to see how it plays out. In order for companies to continue to invest time and energy into biosimilars, it has to be worthwhile to make them, Abrams said.

data.title: Axion BioSystems Introduces Synexus, Bringing Richer Functional Insight to Drug Discovery
data.description:
ATLANTA —

Axion BioSystems, a leading provider of advanced live-cell analysis technology, today announced the launch of Synexus, a first-of-its-kind platform for disease research and therapeutic development. Synexus brings single-cell resolution to high-throughput, label-free workflows, helping pharmaceutical researchers generate more informative assays at the scale drug development demands.

The innovative platform combines industry-leading microelectrode array (MEA), next-generation high-density MEA (HD-MEA), and groundbreaking electrical imaging to connect function and morphology on the same plate. Researchers can investigate cellular activity alongside structural changes across compounds, concentrations, and time points, gathering richer evidence for compound prioritization, neurotoxicity and cardiotoxicity assessment, and mechanistic research.

“Understanding a candidate’s promise and potential liabilities early in development helps pharmaceutical teams make informed decisions before committing to larger, more costly studies,” said Julien Bradley, CEO of Axion BioSystems. “Synexus opens a new chapter in drug screening, bringing single-cell detail and a more connected view of drug response to experiments at scale. We’re expanding what researchers can learn from each assay—and the evidence they can use to decide what moves forward.”

More information from every assay 

As drug development increasingly adopts human cell models and new approach methodologies (NAMs), researchers need assays that capture biological complexity at screening scale. Synexus supports noninvasive assessment of human neural and cardiac cultures, including those derived from induced pluripotent stem cells, allowing scientists to assess disease phenotypes and follow drug responses.

To examine those responses in greater detail, Synexus features Pixel HD technology for HD-MEA and high-content electrical imaging. Together, these capabilities take high-definition analysis beyond electrophysiology to capture cellular activity, organization, and structure.

Across its measurement capabilities, Synexus offers:

  • High-definition analysis at scale: Pixel HD technology provides more than 138,000 electrodes per well at 12.5 µm spacing, bringing single-cell-level spatial detail to high-throughput analysis across 96 wells simultaneously.
  • Connected biological context: Measurements from the same plate help researchers examine how changes in electrophysiology relate to changes in cellular organization.
  • Efficient compound comparisons: Simultaneous recording from up to 96 wells – with 384-well coming soon – keeps treatments, controls and replicates aligned in time.
  • Assay continuity, expanded discovery: Continue established MEA assays used across pharmaceutical safety testing, then add high-definition capabilities to investigate findings more deeply and pursue new lines of inquiry. 
  • Rich datasets for advanced analysis: Functional, spatial and structural measurements provide data for machine learning and AI model development, supporting analysis of drug-response patterns and cellular heterogeneity. 

“In our conversations with scientists, we hear a recurring challenge: getting more information from each assay without making experiments harder to run,” said Stacie Chvatal, Vice President of Product Management at Axion BioSystems. “That feedback helped shape Synexus. We’re bringing cellular activity and structural context together so teams can better understand a compound’s effects across the conditions and replicates their studies require.”

Built for today’s assays and tomorrow’s applications

Researchers can configure Synexus around established assays, then add measurement capabilities, analysis tools, plate formats, and workflows as their programs develop. This expandable architecture helps laboratories protect their investment while pursuing new applications.

Synexus builds on more than 15 years of Axion BioSystems’ experience and an established live-cell analysis ecosystem that includes more than 1,500 systems installed worldwide and thousands of peer-reviewed publications using Axion technology. Axion’s industry-leading Maestro MEA technology has an established track record in pharmaceutical safety research, with widespread adoption among leading drug developers.

To learn more, visit the Synexus product page.

data.title: Drugs from China are reshaping biotech. Track the licensing deals here.
data.description:
The makeup of the world’s pharmaceutical pipeline is changing. China’s fast-growing biotechnology industry is a big reason why. 

Over the past decade, China’s government has sought to upgrade the country’s drugmaking capabilities. Its efforts birthed a burgeoning ecosystem of homegrown companies and science parks that mirror — and even rival —  U.S. hubs in Boston and San Francisco. Lower costs and regulatory flexibility have helped China’s biotech startups move faster than their U.S. counterparts, producing a sprawling inventory of drug prospects. While many are designed to be superior versions of medicines either on the market or in development elsewhere, more and more are innovative, challenging the U.S.’s long-held biotech advantage. 

Large pharma companies and venture capital investors have taken note. Many are licensing experimental drugs from China, either to add to their drug portfolios or build new biotechs around. The shift has been rapid, with dealmaking spiking in recent years. According to analysts, licensing agreements hit a record pace in 2025. Fully one-third of the industry’s licensing spending in 2025 involved drugs sourced from China, per the investment bank Jefferies. That trajectory has accelerated in 2026.

These deals reveal important insights about the types of medicines drugmakers and investors want in their portfolios. With this database, we’re tracking deals from 2025 onward in which China-based drugmakers licensed to U.S. and European companies rights to human therapeutics. We show the companies involved, the financial terms of their alliances and details about the medicines and drug targets. 

If we’ve missed a deal, or there’s any additional information you’d like to see, please reach out and let us know.

Jump to database

Jump to methodology

Complex antibodies and small molecules are a popular target

Licensing agreements announced in 2025 and 2026

Cancer, immune disease drugs are drawing the most interest

Licensing agreements announced in 2025 and 2026

Deals typically involve early-stage drug candidates

Licensing agreements announced in 2025 and 2026

Licensing deals are getting bigger in size and scope

Licensing deals involving China-developed drugs

Database includes deals announced in 2025 and 2026 that involve a China-based biotechnology firm licensing a drug candidate or candidates to biopharmaceutical companies located in the U.S. or Europe.

Methodology

For this database, BioPharma Dive compiled deals announced in 2025 and 2026 through which China-based drugmakers licensed out innovative human medicines to biotech or pharmaceutical companies in the U.S. or Europe. 

We screened for these deals in company press releases, analyst reports and on social media sites like LinkedIn. We eliminated those that didn’t meet our criteria, including alliances that don’t mention any specific drug candidates or partnerships between two China-based companies. We also excluded deals involving generic drugs or biosimilars.

We generally used a deal’s most advanced program to determine the therapeutic area of focus, treatment type and stage of development at the time of a deal’s announcement. We categorized phase of development by the latest stage underway at the time of a deal.

Therapeutic areas cover a large number of diseases and, in some cases, overlap. In most cases, when companies identified more than one therapeutic area with equal priority, we classified them as working on “multiple” therapeutic areas. Companies that identified multiple areas, but prioritized one over others were classified under that priority area.

Ned Pagliarulo contributed reporting.

data.title: Breaking the silos: What effective scenario modeling looks like in 2026 and beyond
data.description:
International reference pricing has been a talking point for elected officials and Department of Health and Human Services leaders in the U.S. for nearly a decade, but President Donald Trump’s May 2025 executive order pushed for broader and faster adoption than many industry experts anticipated.

By the end of 2025, 14 of the 17 large drugmakers addressed by the White House had signed voluntary agreements to offer newly launched medicines in the U.S. at prices comparable to those in other high-income countries and make existing drugs available to Medicaid patients at most-favored-nation (MFN) prices. The three remaining manufacturers soon followed, along with nine other companies, bringing participation up to approximately 89% of the branded market in just over a year of the executive order’s publication. An early signal of MFN’s impact is an apparent decrease in new drug launches in EU markets, with one source estimating that launches declined roughly 35% year over year during that time period.

The introduction of MFN pricing represents one of the most consequential changes to pricing and access policies the U.S. pharmaceutical market has seen in years, but it is by no means the only major shift across the commercialization landscape. The EU’s Joint Clinical Assessment (JCA) process is raising the bar for comparative evidence standards, while national Health Technology Assessment (HTA) bodies such as NICE and Germany’s G-BA are scrutinizing evidence more closely and making greater use of real-world evidence (RWE) to supplement clinical trial data. Around the globe, market forces and supply chains are becoming increasingly volatile and interdependent. As they do, pharmaceutical decision-makers must navigate increasingly complex trade-offs with significant downside risk.

“Today’s complexity means that pharmaceutical leaders can no longer think in terms of sequential steps when they’re planning a launch strategy,” said Michael Day, Ph.D., senior director of regulatory strategy and CMC at Cencora. “You can’t optimize your regulatory path and then product safety and then market access and commercialization and expect the best possible global outcome. Sometimes the best regulatory path is not the best path to the market. In this world, all the different disciplines need to work together for a common cause.”

Scenario modeling — the practice of building and testing multiple forecasts based on a variety of assumptions about policies, competition and global markets — is an essential tool for decision-makers tasked with charting a course through these kinds of uncertainties. But most pharmaceutical companies still model scenarios using a single-threaded approach — that is, one function at a time — with each department working in isolation, using its own model and assumptions.

What’s needed for success is an integrated approach to scenario modeling and analysis, one that incorporates data gathered across the entire organization, breaks down the silos between departments and disciplines, and leverages newer technologies such as AI to manage the additional complexity.

Planning for commercialization in a borderless global market

JCA provides a joint scientific assessment of the relative clinical effectiveness and safety of a medicine compared with alternatives, but it does not determine pricing, reimbursement or overall value. National HTA bodies are required to give the JCA due consideration during their own country-specific assessments, alongside economic, healthcare-system and other concerns. A JCA report showing uncertainty about comparators, endpoints or generalizability can make payers more cautious and weaken your value story. Manufacturers need to consider this interdependency from the earliest phases of development.

They should also design an evidence plan that will satisfy both national payers and regulators. A clinical development program may be sufficient to support regulatory approval but still leave gaps for JCA or national HTA if it does not generate the comparative evidence needed against relevant standards of care. And because JCA is now conducted in parallel with EMA review, that evidence must be ready at the time of submission.

“In the past, manufacturers could choose which countries to make HTA submissions in, and they could base this decision on what kinds of data they had available,” explained Casper Paardekooper, vice president for health policy and strategy at Cencora. “Now, when they take part in the European clinical assessment process, as many as 27 different countries can have input into the PICOs (Population, Intervention, Comparator and Outcome) that serve as evidence in the JCA. To be successful in this process, you have to plan to include an array of comparators, endpoints and subpopulations in your research, and you need to have the evidence ready early on.”

In the current climate, European national pricing outcomes can not only sway other EU countries’ HTA bodies but also influence negotiations elsewhere, including the U.S. Prices in other parts of the world are interconnected, too. Several countries in Southeast Asia use reference pricing based on prices in European countries, while Australia is a major reference input for Canada.

“MFN and international reference pricing mean that what we do in one local market no longer only has local consequences,” Day said.

Reimagining scenario modeling for this new era

Many drugmakers still maintain separate U.S. and European launch teams, with each conducting its own pricing research and payer intelligence. In today’s world, the potential trade-offs involved in launch sequencing make this traditional approach untenable.

In integrated scenario modeling, policy, regulatory and CMC, market access, medical, clinical, and pharmacovigilance teams all provide input, making it possible to test scenarios that no single function could evaluate on its own:

  • If you launch first in the U.S., should you still launch in Europe, Japan and Canada?
  • If so, in what order?
  • How much U.S. pricing risk can you accept in exchange for greater volume in Europe?

AI-enabled analytics can help make integrated scenario modeling more scalable by synthesizing large amounts of data and evidence, allowing teams to interrogate a broader range of scenarios than would be practical manually. It can also help teams update those scenarios more efficiently as assumptions, evidence and market conditions change.

AI doesn’t replace expert judgment, though. “AI can generate a plethora of different scenarios, but human experts still need to understand what those scenarios mean,” Day said. “The greater the uncertainty, the greater the diversity of thinking that’s required. Pharmaceutical companies will need to become increasingly agile and able to pivot quickly as soon as regulatory requirements or markets change.”

“Increasingly, strategic foresight is becoming the most critical capability within a pharmaceutical company,” Paardekooper added.

Start early

Integrated planning is best initiated in the earliest stages of product development. By launch day, it’s far too late to make critical changes in endpoint selection or clinical data strategies. Maximizing the return on your investments in R&D requires getting new treatments to patients as soon as possible. Without an interdisciplinary, connected strategy, there’s a risk of delay — or even that patients will not have access to the new therapy at all.

“The earlier you think about these things, and put them together, the more flexibility you can build into your development program,” Day added. “This flexibility enables drugmakers to make critical decisions with greater visibility into their downstream consequences. This is the foundation of success.”

Learn more about the market forces reshaping global launch strategies in Cencora’s latest report.

data.title: mzio launches first vendor-neutral AI control layer for multimodal mass spectrometry data processing
data.description:
BREMEN, Germany —

mzio GmbH announces the launch of mzassist, a vendor-neutral AI and automation control layer for multimodal mass spectrometry data processing on its trusted, open-source mzmine platform.

mzassist uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP) open standard introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, now supported by many AI agents and platforms, to connect mzio’s established, vendor-agnostic mzmine platform to a user’s approved MCP-compatible AI assistant. For the lab user, this simplifies set up and implementation of complete mass spectrometry data processing workflows in natural language; importing raw data, selecting templates, configuring parameters, running batches and summarizing results to increase operational consistency and free up lab time to focus on scientific input. 

mzio shared exclusive preview access to mzassist with the scientific community in a workshop at the 8th Munich Metabolomics Meeting on October 13th, 2026, ahead of public release, giving researchers hands-on experience with the technology in LC-MS, GC-MS and MALDI-MS and gaining valuable feedback. 

The mzassist approach draws a clear line on security and scientific control in the laboratory: the raw mass spec data stays on the lab’s own computer, and users control the information that is shared with the AI via opt-in / opt-out protocols. Because the AI tool is only active when enabled by the user, the user decides at every stage how much to hand over, either delegating the entire workflow or enabling manual intervention at any stage. Parameter decisions are made by deterministic mzmine algorithms rather than the language model, and labs connect the AI assistant that their IT and data protection teams have already approved, increasing accessibility and speed for mass spectrometry data management. 

“The AI story in lab informatics has now moved from ‘can we use it?’ to ‘how do we use it responsibly?’” Dr. Ansgar Korf, CEO and co-founder of mzio comments. “mzassist brings together two key factors in mass spectrometry data management: the reliability of our long established, trusted mzmine system to handle the scientific decisions, and new accessibility through AI. The lab chooses which AI assistant to trust, and mzmine stays the authoritative environment for the data analysis itself. That combination makes AI practical in a mass spec workflow without compromising reproducibility or the vendor-neutral position that mzmine has held since 2005.”

mzassist can also help lab users get started faster with both existing and new analytical methods, explaining processing steps, algorithms and parameters, and supporting spectral library building. The parameter estimator analyzes a selection of the user’s raw data files and derives suitable processing parameters, and the auto optimizer then benchmarks and identifies the settings that perform best on the actual data. 

“Parameter estimation and optimization in mzassist are data-driven algorithms, not guesswork by a language model,” adds Dr. Steffen Heuckeroth, CTO and co-founder of mzio. “The estimator derives parameters directly from the signals in a lab’s raw data, with consistent results every time. Users and AI agents can both call on these tools to get the same measurable basis for deciding which parameters to use, and every analysis started through mzassist is documented as a complete mzmine workflow file that records each processing step and parameter, meaning AI assistance increases productivity while keeping results reproducible and traceable." 

mzassist will be available with mzmine 4.11 October 2026. Laboratories can connect the AI tool that fits their own IT, data protection and compliance requirements. It is included in mzmine COMMUNITY for academic users and in mzmine PRO for commercial customers, supporting mzio’s mission to empower researchers and analysts around the world with reliable tools for mass spectrometry data analysis. More information is available at mzio.io.

data.title: Flagship blends three biotech startups to form Etcelera
data.description:
The biotechnology startup creator Flagship Pioneering is rolling three of its fledgling companies into a new venture called Etcelera, which is combining artificial intelligence with an array of drug discovery tools to try to predict which experimental medicines might succeed in the clinic.

Flagship announced Thursday that the new startup has been formed from the parts of three former portfolio companies: Etiome, Cellarity and Empress Therapeutics. It’s led by Adrian “Ad” Rawcliffe, the former CEO of Adaptimmune and a veteran of GSK.

“Each had a piece of this puzzle, and if you bring them together, then we have the opportunity to go beyond what each of them was doing and redefine cause-and-effect in biology,” Rawcliffe said in an interview.

Etcelera claims that combining the technologies of these three companies with Flagship’s in-house AI capabilities should help its scientists pinpoint novel disease drivers and uncover small molecule medicines to target them. It also believes these drugs will have better odds than those discovered with traditional approaches. Rawcliffe said the datasets and technology developed by its three forebears could be useful in gauging which drugs might fail in human testing.

“If you feed appropriate machine learning enough biological language, then maybe it can infer what biology looks like, where meaning lies in biology and can predict what will happen in biological systems,” Rawcliffe said.

Biotech companies have long spoken enthusiastically about the ability of high-powered computing tools to upend drug discovery and cure many diseases. The hype has sparked blowback that companies using AI to design medicines may be overstating their potential and underestimating the complexities of human biology. Multiple biotechs built on AI technology have struggled in the public markets. 

Yet private investment in AI drug discovery companies has accelerated in 2026. Several have raised large funding rounds, and one company, Iambic Therapeutics, recently went public. (AI giant Anthropic, which has invested heavily in life sciences research, could soon follow.) 

Etcelera is combining AI tools with a series of other strategies. And one edge Rawcliffe believes the company has is its use of “perturbation data,” a way of seeing how a cell would respond to disruption, such as by silencing a gene or introducing a chemical.

The company intends to develop medicines for hematological conditions, immune diseases and metabolic-fibrotic disorders. It’s starting out with a handful of programs for conditions such as myelofibrosis and essential thrombocythemia.

“Our vision is to build a compounding AI system that becomes a definitive source of novel medicines that are more likely to succeed in clinical development than any prior technology,” said Alec Reynolds, a senior partner at Flagship and chair of Etcelera’s board, in a statement.

Flagship will shuttle an oral sickle cell disease drug that Cellarity discovered into a different, standalone company, the firm said.

No new funding was announced alongside Etcelera’s public launch. The three biotechs it’s built on had banked $374 million in venture capital backing prior to the merger, which Rawcliffe said will help carry the company further.

The new biotech will retain a 2022 partnership between Novo and Cellarity formed to find a small molecule treatment for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis. A second alliance with an unnamed large pharmaceutical firm is also in the works, Rawcliffe said.

“We’ll be looking for partners who bring substantial disease or therapy area expertise to pair with this platform,” he said.

Etcelera’s name is a kind of portmanteau of “et cetera” and “accelerate,” an idea Rawcliffe said was born out of the theory that simulating early drug development on a computer could speed up the iterative process of finding new drugs.
